options: A program that runs too slowly
A bug in which the result depends on the order in which threads access shared data
questions.explain: The outcome changes from run to run, which makes these bugs hard to find.

questions.prompt: Two threads each run `counter++` 100000 times on a shared `int` with no protection. What is guaranteed?
options: It prints a number between 100000 and 200000
Nothing precise: it may print less than 200000
questions.explain: `counter++` is read, add, write. Two threads can read the same value and one update is lost.

questions.prompt: A shared variable is declared `volatile int j`. Why does `j = j + 1` from two threads still lose updates?
options: `volatile` forces memory accesses but does not make read-add-write atomic
questions.explain: `volatile` is not synchronisation. The slides use it in the racy example and the examples that are fixed by a mutex or a semaphore: the fix is the lock, not the keyword.

questions.prompt: A correct solution to the critical section problem must provide:
options: That the section runs in under a millisecond
questions.explain: Mutual exclusion (one at a time), progress (the decision to enter is not postponed forever) and bounded waiting (no thread waits forever).
option_notes: False: speed is not a requirement.

questions.prompt: What does `pthread_mutex_lock` do when another thread holds the mutex?
options: Blocks until the mutex is free
questions.explain: The thread sleeps until the owner unlocks.
The access to the shared variable must be between the lock and the unlock.

questions.prompt: `pthread_mutex_trylock` returns {{0}} (an error name) when the mutex is already held by another thread.
questions.explain: It returns 0 when it got the mutex.

questions.prompt: Thread 1 locks mutex A and then B; thread 2 locks B and then A. What can happen?
options: A deadlock: each holds one and waits for the other
questions.explain: This is the classic lock-ordering deadlock.

questions.prompt: What is the simplest way to avoid that deadlock?
options: Always take the locks in the same order in every thread
questions.explain: If every thread locks A before B, nobody can hold B while waiting for A.

questions.prompt: Put the parts of a critical section in order.
items: Read and change the shared data
Continue with code that does not use the shared data
questions.explain: Keep what is between lock and unlock as short as possible.

questions.prompt: Match each function with its purpose.
pairs: takes the mutex, waiting if needed
takes the mutex only if it is free
frees the mutex when it is no longer used
questions.explain: Initialise once, lock and unlock around each critical section, destroy at the end.

questions.prompt: What is the main difference between a mutex and a binary semaphore?
options: A mutex has an owner: only the thread that locked it may unlock it
questions.explain: The slides call a binary semaphore a "mutex". In POSIX they are different: a semaphore can be posted by any thread, which makes it useful for signalling.

questions.prompt: A thread locks a normal mutex it already holds. What happens?
options: It blocks forever, waiting for itself
questions.explain: With the default type there is no recursion: the thread deadlocks itself.

questions.prompt: One function updates `count` under a mutex; another function updates `count` without any lock. Is the program correct?
options: Yes, one protected access is enough
No: every access to the shared data must use the same lock
Yes, if the other function is short
questions.explain: Mutual exclusion only works when all the accesses take part.
